summary: This Informational document reports on the IAB's AI-CONTROL workshop held in September 2024. It summarizes the main points of discussion and topics that may need more work. The views are the participants' and do not necessarily reflect the IAB's.

plainLanguage.summary: A meeting about how website owners can say what AI programs may do with their pages, with notes of what people said.

questions: how to control ai use of web content
how do website owners control ai use
what is wrong with robots.txt for ai
how can ai preferences be embedded in content
subtitle: Standardizing how website owners communicate preferences about AI training and use.

tldr.problem: Website owners want to control how artificial intelligence companies crawl and use their content, but there is no coordinated standard. Different AI vendors interpret robots.txt differently, and existing mechanisms like robots.txt have significant limitations for this use case.
tldr.mechanism: The IAB convened the AI-CONTROL Workshop to explore practical opt-out mechanisms and understand what a standardized approach should look like, considering attachment mechanisms (where preferences are placed), vocabulary (what opt-out means), and how preferences are enforced.
tldr.outcome: The workshop identified that robots.txt alone is insufficient and proposed IETF work on attachment methods, embedding preferences in IETF-controlled formats (like HTTP headers), defining a common vocabulary, and specifying how multiple preference mechanisms combine.

today: RFC 9969 is an Informational report from May 2026 that reflects the consensus and outstanding questions from the IAB's AI-CONTROL Workshop. It provides guidance for future IETF standardization work on AI content preferences, while acknowledging that broader legal and policy questions remain beyond the scope of technical standards.

sections.title: The AI-CONTROL Workshop
sections.content:
The IAB convened the AI-CONTROL Workshop in September 2024 to address a growing problem: website owners and AI vendors have conflicting interests regarding the crawling and use of web content for artificial intelligence training. The Internet has become a major source of training data for Large Language Models (LLMs) and other AI systems, but this use was not envisioned by most content publishers.

In response, content owners have adopted various practices—terms of service, embedded metadata, robots.txt, paywalls, and IP blocking—to express preferences about AI use. However, these practices lack coordination and standardization. The workshop brought together technical experts, AI vendors, content publishers, civil society advocates, and policymakers to "explore practical opt-out mechanisms for AI and build an understanding of use cases, requirements, and other considerations."
sections.plainLanguage: AI companies need text from websites to train their AI. Website owners want a say in whether their content gets used. The workshop tried to figure out a fair way for both sides to communicate.

sections.title: The Crawl Time vs. Inference Time Problem
sections.content:
The core challenge is the disconnect between when a website owner expresses a preference and when it can be enforced. Website owners can attach preferences to their content at crawl time (when a crawler visits and fetches content) through mechanisms like robots.txt or embedded metadata. However, these preferences often cannot be applied at inference time (when a trained AI model is used).

Once content has been used to train an AI model, the trained model does not distinguish which training data came from which sources or which preferences applied to that data. Therefore, an AI vendor that wants to honor a content owner's preference (such as "non-commercial use only" or "no military use") faces unappealing choices: either omit that data from the foundation model (reducing its viability) or create separate models for each preference combination (leading to model proliferation). This fundamental mismatch between the statement of preferences and their enforceability undermines trust in the entire system.
sections.plainLanguage: When a website says "don't use my content for military purposes," an AI company cannot actually enforce that after the AI learns. The trained AI doesn't remember which website each fact came from. So either the AI company ignores the request or makes a separate version of AI just for that rule.

sections.title: Attachment Mechanisms: Where Preferences Live
sections.content:
A major focus of the workshop was attachment—how preferences are associated with content. Several mechanisms were discussed.

robots.txt (the Robots Exclusion Protocol) is widely recognized but has deficiencies. It does not scale to granular control within large sites (such as YouTube, where different creators have different policies). Site administrators may not allow individual creators to express preferences. If content moves to another site, robots.txt preferences are not automatically transferred. Additionally, different AI vendors interpret robots.txt inconsistently.

Embedding preferences directly in content (using HTML <meta> tags, image metadata, XML/JSON extensions) has advantages: it travels with content when copied or moved offline. However, embedded metadata is easily stripped during file optimization or privacy-protection processes, and some content types (plain text, social media feeds with multiple creators) cannot easily embed metadata.

Registries (centralized databases matched by content fingerprint, like those used in music publishing) decouple content from its location. However, deploying registries at Internet scale has proven problematic and does not align well with how the open web operates.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop discussed three ways to attach preferences: robots.txt (a text file at the website root), embedding preferences inside the content itself, or using a registry like a phonebook. Each method has problems.

sections.title: Vocabulary and Trust Issues
sections.content:
A secondary focus was vocabulary—what specific opt-out signals mean. There are already many proposals for vocabularies, and conflicting interpretations exist. The workshop found general agreement that a complex vocabulary is unlikely to succeed, implying that simplicity is essential.

Beyond technical mechanisms, trust emerged as a critical issue. Content owners lack confidence in the system because there is no way to monitor whether AI vendors are honoring preferences, no attribution of data sources in LLMs, and no enforcement mechanism. This lack of trust has driven increasingly aggressive measures by publishers: IP address blocking, paywalls, and other active blocking of AI crawlers. Participants noted that "robots.txt is broken and we broke it," suggesting the current ecosystem is unsustainable for everyone.
sections.plainLanguage: Everyone also needs to agree on what "don't use this" means, since different companies might interpret it differently. And website owners don't trust that AI companies will follow the rules since nobody can check if they do.

sections.title: Standards Work and Open Questions
sections.content:
The workshop ended with general agreement that positive technical steps are possible, despite legal and fundamental limitations of opt-out regimes. The IETF can contribute through several specific areas: (1) attachment to websites by location (robots.txt or similar mechanism); (2) attachment via embedding in IETF-controlled formats, such as HTTP headers; (3) definition of a common core vocabulary; and (4) definition of the overall regime, specifying how preferences from multiple attachment mechanisms are combined and which ones take precedence.

Explicitly out of scope for initial work are enforcement mechanisms, registry-based solutions, crawler identification and authentication, and transparency or audit mechanisms. The workshop recognized that while technical standards alone cannot solve all problems (legal uncertainty and the crawl-time vs. inference-time mismatch remain fundamental challenges), coordinating on attachment and vocabulary will improve the situation significantly.
sections.plainLanguage: The group decided to start with simpler, more practical standards: how to attach preferences to websites, what the preferences mean, and what to do when there are multiple ways to say the same thing. They did not try to solve checking whether AI companies followed the rules.
